summary_html: Agency decides to **remove a child immediately** due to **imminent danger** prior to a court order. Federal law (ASFA/IV-E) requires later **court findings** on reasonable efforts; constitutional limits (due process; search/seizure) apply.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E (42 U.S.C. §§ 670–679c)** — reasonable-efforts findings; permanency timelines  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — monitors safety & removal decision quality

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: Reversing an order of temporary custody, the court held that Connecticut's summary removal scheme is constitutional only because it confines coercive intervention to serious physical illness, serious physical injury or immediate physical danger and requires that measures short of removal be used where possible.
key_cases.relevance: It sets the constitutional ceiling on the emergency removal decision and reverses a removal made on 'subjective suspicion' without a showing of immediate risk.
key_cases.quote: This phrase requires that various steps short of removal from the home be used when possible in preference to disturbing the integrity of the family.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Second Circuit held that removing a child on an emergency basis without judicial authorization is unconstitutional when there is reasonable time to obtain a court order safely, and that a state-initiated medical examination of the child implicates Fourth Amendment and bodily integrity interests, although the defendants had qualified immunity because the right was not then clearly established.
key_cases.relevance: It is the governing Second Circuit standard for the emergency removal decision that Connecticut DCF workers are measured against.
key_cases.quote: it is unconstitutional for state officials to effect a child's removal on an "emergency" basis where there is reasonable time safely to obtain judicial authorization consistent with the child's safety

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Second Circuit affirmed summary judgment for Connecticut DCF workers, holding they were entitled to qualified immunity because an objectively reasonable basis existed to believe the children faced an imminent threat when they were removed without parental consent or a court order.
key_cases.relevance: This is the most recent Second Circuit decision squarely reviewing a Connecticut DCF emergency removal decision.
key_cases.quote: In sum, notwithstanding the evidence plaintiffs claim the District Court overlooked or misconstrued, we readily conclude that the defendants are entitled to qualified immunity here.

key_cases.holding: Answering certified questions from the federal District Court in a suit by children who were left in an abusive home, the court held that § 17a-101g (c) is directory rather than mandatory, so that on probable cause of imminent risk of physical harm the commissioner is authorized but not required to invoke a ninety-six hour hold and may instead choose among the other statutory protective remedies.
key_cases.relevance: It holds that the emergency removal decision is discretionary, so a caseworker who declines to remove has not violated § 17a-101g (c).
key_cases.quote: § 17a-101g (c) does not require the commissioner to remove the child upon a finding of probable cause, but merely authorizes the commissioner to seek removal under such circumstances.

key_cases.holding: The court held that parents stated a justiciable claim for declaratory and injunctive relief against the systemic failure to provide timely evidentiary hearings on orders of temporary custody, and that the trial court improperly struck their request for relief.
key_cases.relevance: The emergency removal decision is constitutionally tolerable only if followed by a prompt adversarial hearing, which is what this case enforces.
key_cases.quote: It is precisely because state intervention can cause irrevocable consequences for both children and parents that "fundamentally fair" procedures provided in a timely manner must be afforded the parties.

state_agency.name: Connecticut Department of Children and Families
state_agency.hotline: 1-800-842-2288 (DCF Careline, 24 hours a day, every day of the year); TDD 1-800-624-5518

investigation_requirements: Any visit to or evaluation of a home conducted pursuant to a safety plan must be conducted in person, unless a resident of the home is subject to an order of quarantine or isolation (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 17a-101t, P.A. 24-92, effective July 1, 2024)

timeline_requirements.starts_from: Child removed without a court order
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: If the child is not returned home within 96 hours, DCF must proceed in court under Conn. Gen. Stat. § 46b-129

notice_requirements.timing: With service of an ex parte order of temporary custody or order to appear; preliminary hearing held not later than 10 days after the order issues
content_required: Conspicuous notice written in clear and simple language
That the order contains allegations that conditions in the home have endangered the safety and welfare of the child or youth
That a hearing will be held on the date on the form and is the parents' opportunity to present their position on the alleged facts
That an attorney will be appointed for parents who cannot afford one, and how and where to apply, as soon as possible so counsel can prepare

That the parents or a person responsible for the child may ask the Commissioner of Children and Families to investigate placing the child with a blood or marriage relative as licensed foster parent or temporary custodian
That parents with questions about the case or appointment of counsel should go to the court or call the clerk's office as soon as possible
notice_requirements.defective_notice_consequence: Not specified in Conn. Gen. Stat. § 46b-129(b)

statutory_basis.citation_text: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 46b-129(b) (order of temporary custody or order to appear; required conspicuous notice to the respondent; preliminary hearing not later than ten days after issuance)
